questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman is brought in after an intentional ingestion. She has slurred speech, dilated pupils, temperature 40 °C, BP 150/90, HR 120, and RR 36. Which class of agent best explains these findings?
questions.explanation: Mydriasis, hyperthermia, tachycardia, and hypertension point to a stimulant (FAST: free-base cocaine, anticholinergics, sympathomimetics, theophylline). A: Opioids cause miosis, bradypnea, and hypothermia. B: Benzodiazepines cause sedation without hyperthermia or tachycardia. C: Organophosphates cause SLUDGE with miosis and bradycardia. E: β-blockers cause bradycardia and hypotension.

questions.stem: On the lecture's lists of agents causing toxic hypotension and toxic bradycardia, which agent appears on both?
questions.explanation: Clonidine (with calcium channel blockers) is listed for both hypotension and bradycardia. B: Cocaine (free base) causes tachycardia and hyperthermia. C: Theophylline also causes tachycardia and hyperthermia. D: Reserpine is listed for hypotension only. E: Digoxin is listed for bradycardia only.

questions.stem: A patient presents 6 hours after swallowing a large number of tablets. Which statement about emptying the stomach (emesis or lavage) is most accurate?

options.A: It should be done before assessing airway and circulation
options.B: It is most effective 4–8 hours after ingestion
options.C: It enhances elimination of drug already absorbed
options.D: It must be done before any antidote can be given
options.E: Its benefit is now limited; it works mainly within 1–2 hours

questions.explanation: Emptying the stomach is effective only 1–2 h after ingestion; by 6 h most drug has left the stomach. A: Stabilizing vital signs (ABC) always comes first. B: The useful window is 1–2 h, not 4–8 h. C: It prevents absorption; enhanced elimination uses forced diuresis, multiple-dose charcoal, dialysis, hemoperfusion or urine alkalinization. D: Antidotes are given as soon as indicated; they must be used quickly.

questions.stem: Naloxone reverses opioid toxicity by competing at μ-opioid receptors. How is it classified among antidote mechanisms?
questions.explanation: Antidotes that act on receptors are pharmacological antidotes; naloxone displaces opioids from μ receptors. A: Chemical antidotes inactivate the poison itself (e.g., chelators, N-acetylcysteine detoxifying NAPQI). B: Functional antagonists reverse downstream effects through another mechanism. D: Chelators bind metals. E: Elimination enhancers include dialysis, charcoal, and urine alkalinization.

questions.stem: A patient overdoses on a drug with strong antimuscarinic effects. He has hot dry skin, dilated pupils, tachycardia, and urinary retention. Which antidote is indicated?
questions.explanation: Physostigmine, a cholinesterase inhibitor, raises acetylcholine and overcomes the muscarinic block. A: Atropine is itself antimuscarinic and would worsen this; it treats cholinergic (organophosphate) poisoning. C: Naloxone reverses opioids. D: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines. E: Acetylcysteine treats acetaminophen poisoning.

questions.stem: An unresponsive patient arrives with an unknown ingestion. His respirations are shallow and BP is 80/50. What should be done first?

options.A: Identify the exact toxic agent with a urine drug screen

questions.explanation: Treat the patient, not the poison: maintaining respiration and circulation comes first. A: Identification proceeds in parallel and often only the class is found. B: Antidotes must have a clearly defined indication and can themselves be toxic. C: Decontamination follows stabilization and is time-limited. D: Enhanced elimination is for selected poisons after stabilization.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old farmer collapses after spraying crops with an organophosphate. He has salivation, lacrimation, urination, diarrhea, vomiting, pinpoint pupils, and bradycardia. Which antidote should be given?
questions.explanation: Organophosphates inhibit acetylcholinesterase, causing cholinergic excess (SLUDGE, miosis, bradycardia); atropine blocks the muscarinic effects. A: Physostigmine also inhibits acetylcholinesterase and would worsen toxicity. C: Naloxone is for opioids; pinpoint pupils alone don't make this opioid toxicity, and opioids don't cause SLUDGE. D: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines. E: Desferrioxamine treats iron poisoning.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old is brought in after swallowing many of his pregnant mother's prenatal vitamins. He has vomiting, bloody diarrhea, and lethargy, with metabolic acidosis. Which antidote is indicated?
questions.explanation: Iron overdose (GI hemorrhage, then acidosis and shock) is treated with the iron chelator deferoxamine. A: Succimer chelates lead and other heavy metals. B: NAC treats acetaminophen. D: Methylene blue treats methemoglobinemia. E: Fomepizole treats methanol and ethylene glycol.

questions.stem: A patient is admitted with a large aspirin overdose. Which measure from the lecture enhances aspirin elimination?

options.A: Sodium bicarbonate infusion to alkalinize the urine

questions.explanation: Alkaline urine ionizes the weak acid aspirin, trapping it in the tubule so more is excreted. B: Acid urine keeps aspirin un-ionized, so more is reabsorbed. C: Stomach emptying works only within 1–2 h. D: Desferrioxamine chelates iron. E: Ethanol is the antidote for methanol and ethylene glycol.
